---
title: "Pop Singing: Speech, Mix, Runs and the Mic"
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

Pop singing sounds like talking on pitch. The words come first, the tone stays close to your speaking voice, and the style lives in small things: how a note starts, a little cry or breath, a run at the end of a line. This lesson builds those things one at a time, from breathing to riffs and harmony.

**How to use the page.** Each exercise has a staff and a ▶ button. The exercises are written for a middle voice. Choose **Your voice** once and every exercise moves into your range; men read treble-clef notes an octave lower, as usual. Exercises marked *Step up* climb a half step each time you press it, the way a warm-up works through the range. Click a heading to fold a section away.

::: {.vx-care}
**Look after your voice.** Warm up before you sing hard, and stop if anything hurts, tickles or feels tight. Hoarseness after singing means you pushed too much. Drink water, and rest a tired voice rather than singing through it. If hoarseness lasts more than two weeks, see a doctor.
:::

## Breath and posture

Stand as if you were about to talk to a friend across the room: feet under the hips, knees soft, head level, shoulders loose. Breathe in low and quietly, so the belly and lower ribs widen and the shoulders don't rise. Then let the air out slowly and steadily, without squeezing.

**Exercise:** hiss out on "sss" for a count of 8, then 12, then 16, keeping the sound even. Then do the same on a hum.

The aim isn't a huge breath. It's a steady one you don't have to fight.

## Starting the note: the onset

A note can start three ways:

- **Breathy:** air first, then sound, as in a sigh, "hhhey".
- **Hard:** a little click of the vocal folds first, as in "uh-oh!".
- **Balanced:** air and sound together.

Pop uses all three for effect, but a balanced onset is home base. Sing the five notes below on "mum", starting each note gently with the M.

<div class="abc-ex" data-loop="up"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
C D E F | G F E D | C4 |]
w: mum mum mum mum mum mum mum mum mum
</script></div>

Now sing the first note three times, once with each onset: "hhhum", "'um" and "um". Hear the difference, then go back to the balanced one.

## Speech level and the mix

Your speaking voice and your high, light voice (head voice) join somewhere around the middle of your range. Pop singers keep the sound speech-like through that join. That blend is the **mix**. The safest way to find it is with exercises that keep the throat easy: lip trills (a horse's "brrr") and a bratty "nay".

Sing this on a lip trill first, then on "nay" (bright and a bit nasal, like a teasing kid). Let the sound stay small at the top. Don't shout up there.

<div class="abc-ex" data-loop="up"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C2 E2 G2 c2 | G2 E2 C4 |]
w: nay nay nay nay nay nay nay
</script></div>

As you step up, the top note will want to "flip" into a lighter sound. Let it flip at first. Over weeks, the "nay" helps the flip smooth out into a mix.

::: {.vx-tip}
If your jaw juts or your neck tightens at the top, go back down two steps and make the sound smaller. Pop high notes come from a lighter, more speech-like voice, not from more push.
:::

## Vowels and words

Sing the words the way you'd say them: "love" is "luv", not an operatic "lahv". Two habits help.

- **Sing on the vowel and get to the consonant late.** In "night", hold "ah" and save the "-eet" ending for the very end of the note.
- **Narrow the vowel a little on high notes.** "Ah" leans toward "uh", and "ee" toward "ih". The word still reads, and the throat stays easier.

Sing this line on "I can't stop thinking 'bout you", holding the vowels and putting the consonants late.

<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
z2 E2 G2 G2 | A3 G E2 D2 | C6 z2 |]
w: I can't stop think-ing 'bout you
</script></div>

## Belt, carefully

**Belting** is the strong, speech-like sound of pop and musical theatre on high notes, like a call across a playground: "Hey!". Done well it is bright and forward, not shouted. Keep it short at first, and keep it well inside your comfort zone.

<div class="abc-ex" data-loop="up"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
G2 E2 | C4 |]
w: Hey! hey! hey!
</script></div>

::: {.vx-care}
Belt for a few minutes at a time, not a whole session. If you feel any squeeze in your throat, go back to "nay" (the previous section). A teacher in person is the best guide for belting.
:::

## Riffs and runs

A **run** is a quick string of notes on one syllable, usually at the end of a phrase. Most pop runs come from the pentatonic scale. Learn each run slowly, on "ah", until every note is clean. Then speed it up.

This run starts on A minor pentatonic: A, C, D, E, G.

<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/16
K:C
Q:1/4=60
e4 dcAG A8 | e2d2c2A2 c2A2G2A2- | A8 z8 |]
w: ah _ _ _ _ ah _ _ _ _ _ _ _
</script></div>

And a common descending one from C major pentatonic: C, D, E, G, A.

<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/16
K:C
Q:1/4=60
c'2a2g2e2 d2c2d2e2 | c8 z8 |]
w: ah _ _ _ _ _ _ _
</script></div>

**Practice:** sing each run at half speed with a metronome, then at full speed. A clean slow run is worth more than a fast blur.

## Style: cry, breath and flips

These colours are what make a singer sound like pop:

- **Cry:** a slight whimper or sob in the tone, like the edge of tears. It lightens the sound and helps it climb.
- **Breathy tone:** let a little air into the start of a quiet phrase for intimacy. Don't use it all the time, or the voice tires.
- **Flip (a yodel break):** let the voice jump into a lighter sound for a moment on the way up, as in many folk and R&B lines.
- **Fry:** the creaky sound at the bottom of the voice, used to start a phrase. Keep it light and brief.

Sing the line below twice: plainly, then adding a flip on the high note and a little breath at the start.

<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
z2 C2 E2 G2 | c4 A2 G2 | E8 |]
w: Oh, I know it's true
</script></div>

## Phrasing and the mic

- **Sit a little behind the beat.** Pop singers often land a word just after the beat, like a relaxed conversation. Try a line both ways with the [Backing Track](../tools/backing-track.qmd) playing.
- **Shape each phrase.** Most lines rise toward an important word and fall away after it.
- **Use the mic.** Sing close (a finger or two away) for quiet, intimate lines. Pull back a few inches for loud notes, so they don't blast. Point the mic at your mouth, not your chin.

## Harmony: singing a third above

Backing vocals often sing a **third above** the melody: two scale steps higher, moving in parallel with it. Sing the melody below, then sing the harmony line written above it.

<div class="abc-ex"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
V:1 name="Harmony"
E F G A | G F E2 |]
V:2 name="Melody"
C D E F | E D C2 |]
</script></div>

**Practice:** play it and sing the melody (the lower line), then the harmony. Then sing the harmony while the recording plays the melody.
